title: The Structure of Academic Prose: Paragraphs, Transitions, and Coherence
paragraphs: A well-structured academic essay is not simply a collection of good ideas arranged in sequence. It is a carefully crafted argument in which each element — each sentence, each paragraph, each transition — contributes to a single coherent purpose. Understanding how to construct this kind of writing requires attention not just to what you say, but to how the parts of your argument relate to each other and to the whole. This relational quality — the way parts connect and serve the whole — is what we mean by coherence.

The paragraph is the fundamental unit of academic prose. Each body paragraph should typically do four things: state its main point in a topic sentence, provide evidence for that point, analyse or explain the evidence in relation to the main claim of the essay, and link to the next paragraph. This structure is sometimes expressed as the "PEEL" method — Point, Evidence, Explain, Link — or similar acronyms, but the labels matter less than the underlying logic. A paragraph that jumps from topic to topic without a clear controlling idea, or that presents evidence without explaining its significance, has failed to do its job.

The topic sentence is particularly important. It should be the most substantive sentence in the paragraph — not a bland statement of intent ("In this paragraph, I will discuss…") but a genuine claim or analytical observation that the rest of the paragraph develops and supports. A well-crafted topic sentence allows a reader to predict what the paragraph will contain and to understand how it connects to the essay's central argument. Reading only the topic sentences of a well-structured essay should give you a clear outline of the argument.

Transitions — words, phrases, and sentences that connect one idea to another — are the connective tissue of academic prose. Within a paragraph, transitional phrases show how sentences relate to each other: "this suggests that," "for example," "in contrast," "as a result," "moreover." Between paragraphs, transitional sentences show how each paragraph connects to the previous one and to the overall argument. A common formula for paragraph transitions is to refer back to the key point of the previous paragraph before introducing the new one, creating a logical chain of reasoning.

Cohesion — the set of linguistic mechanisms that make a text "hang together" as a unified whole rather than a series of disconnected ideas — is related to but distinct from coherence. Coherence is about logical and conceptual organisation; cohesion is about the linguistic devices that express it. Cohesive devices include reference pronouns (using "it," "they," "this" to refer back to previously mentioned concepts), lexical repetition (repeating key terms or using synonyms to maintain focus), and connective adverbs and conjunctions (linking ideas explicitly). Sophisticated academic writing uses all of these to create a seamlessly unified text.

One of the most common weaknesses in student academic writing is what is sometimes called the "list essay" — an essay that consists of a series of discrete points with little or no connection between them, structured like a shopping list rather than an argument. Each point may be individually valid and well-evidenced, but without the argumentative thread that connects them — the "so what?" that shows how each point contributes to the central claim — the essay lacks the analytical depth that distinguishes truly academic writing from mere reportage.

Developing the ability to write coherently and cohesively is a cumulative process. It requires reading widely in your discipline to absorb the conventions of academic prose in that field. It requires attention to how expert writers structure their arguments, manage their evidence, and make their transitions. It requires drafting and revising — not simply producing a first draft and hoping it is good enough, but reading critically what you have produced and asking: Is the argument clear? Is each paragraph doing what it needs to do? Is the evidence sufficient and relevant? Are the connections between ideas explicit and logical? These are the questions of a mature academic writer.

task1Items.question: What are the four functions of a body paragraph according to the text?
task1Items.correct: State main point (topic sentence), provide evidence, analyse/explain the evidence in relation to the central claim, link to the next paragraph

task1Items.question: What is a "topic sentence" and what should it do?
task1Items.correct: The controlling sentence of a paragraph — a genuine claim or analytical observation that the rest of the paragraph develops, allowing readers to predict the content

task1Items.question: What is the difference between coherence and cohesion?
task1Items.correct: Coherence = logical/conceptual organisation; cohesion = linguistic devices (pronouns, connectives, repetition) that express it

task1Items.question: What is a "list essay" and why is it a weakness?
task1Items.correct: A series of discrete valid points without the argumentative thread connecting them — lacks the "so what?" that shows how each contributes to the central claim

task1Items.question: What questions should a mature academic writer ask when revising?
task1Items.correct: Is the argument clear? Is each paragraph doing what it needs to? Is evidence sufficient and relevant? Are connections explicit and logical?
